entry.title: An oral history of Robbie Williams’ Rock DJ video
entry.summary: Creative Process An oral history of Robbie Williams’ Rock DJ video Roller skates, flying flesh and a spot of bother with MTV – director Vaughan Arnell speaks to CR about how he and Robbie Williams created one of pop’s most memorable music videos By Rebecca Fulleylove 05/11/2026 7
entry.content:
Creative Process

An oral history of Robbie Williams’ Rock DJ video

Roller skates, flying flesh and a spot of bother with MTV – director Vaughan Arnell speaks to CR about how he and Robbie Williams created one of pop’s most memorable music videos

By Rebecca Fulleylove 05/11/2026 7:45 am

Few music videos from the turn of the millennium made quite the same impression as Robbie Williams’ Rock DJ. Released in 2000, the promo starts out as a playful disco fantasy before taking a decidedly gruesome turn, as Williams, having failed to attract the attention of the DJ (played by model Ekaterina Ivanova), begins stripping away his own skin, muscle and flesh.

Brilliantly grotesque, it pushed the boundaries of what a mainstream pop video could get away with. MTV’s decision to censor its macabre conclusion only added to the hype, while the video went on to win Best Special Effects in a Video at the MTV Video Music Awards and Best British Video of the Year at the Brit Awards.

Behind the camera was director Vaughan Arnell, whose work has helped shape the visual identity of British pop throughout the 1990s and 2000s. With a career spanning several decades, his credits include videos for the Spice Girls, George Michael, Pet Shop Boys and One Direction, alongside commercials for some of the world’s biggest brands, including Levi’s, Stella Artois, Sky and PureGym.

His long-standing creative partnership with Robbie Williams is among his most celebrated collaborations. Having first worked with Williams during his Take That days, Arnell went on to direct some of the defining videos of his solo career, including Angels, Let Me Entertain You, Millennium, Supreme and Feel. More than 25 years on, Rock DJ remains one of their most memorable projects. Here, Arnell looks back on the creative gambles and on-set chaos during the video’s making, and how the music video industry has changed since.

entry.title: Barbour teams up with Wallace & Gromit for another festive outing
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Barbour teams up with Wallace & Gromit for another festive outing The luxury brand reunites with Aardman for another Wallace & Gromit adventure and shares an exclusive behind-the-scenes look at the craft behind the campaign By Rebecca Fulleylove 05/11/2026 3:
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Barbour teams up with Wallace & Gromit for another festive outing

The luxury brand reunites with Aardman for another Wallace & Gromit adventure and shares an exclusive behind-the-scenes look at the craft behind the campaign

By Rebecca Fulleylove 05/11/2026 3:17 am

Barbour has reunited with Aardman for another Christmas collaboration starring Wallace & Gromit, with the animated duo heading out for an eventful winter walk in the countryside.

Directed by Steve Harding-Hill, the film sees Wallace present Gromit with a Barbour wax dog coat before the pair venture outside to try out his latest invention: the Walk-o-matic. Combining a plump living room armchair with oversized wheels made from Barbour welly boots, the contraption is designed to let Wallace enjoy a countryside stroll without having to take a step himself.

Naturally, things don’t quite go to plan. As the pair make their way through the snow-covered landscape, the Walk-o-matic suffers a series of malfunctions, eventually catapulting Wallace into a mound of snow.

With Wallace left out in the cold, Gromit sees it as the perfect opportunity to present him with his own gift: a Barbour jumper wrapped in tartan. The final Aardman twist comes courtesy of Shaun the Sheep and his flock, who appear with the Walk-o-matic’s welly boots on their heads.

Created using Aardman’s signature stop-motion animation, the film is a character-led celebration of craftsmanship. Barbour has also shared an exclusive behind-the-scenes film with Creative Review [above], offering a closer look at how the adventure was brought to life and the creative process behind it.

This is Barbour’s second Christmas collaboration featuring Wallace & Gromit, and its fourth partnership with Aardman overall. It also continues the brand’s exploration of its Scottish heritage, with its Original and Authentic tartans appearing throughout in the characters’ accessories. The tartans were first showcased in September in a campaign film starring Sienna Miller and Idris Elba.

Alongside the campaign, Barbour has produced a limited-edition run of Re-loved Wallace & Gromit-inspired wax jackets, following last year’s collection. For the first time, the initiative also extends to Re-loved scarves and dog coats, with all proceeds going to Oxfam.

The film is one of a handful of Christmas spots from luxury brands this year that have put an emphasis on the handmade. Veteran Disney director John Pomeroy was enlisted by Prada for an “anti-AI”, hand-drawn tale of winter whimsy, while Dior brought in animation director Sylvain Chomet for its seven-minute short, Night in Color, which opted for a similar fairytale aesthetic.

entry.title: New Edvard Munch exhibition utilises AI and visitor creativity
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration New Edvard Munch exhibition utilises AI and visitor creativity The interactive show allows visitors to create their own artworks, which are then paired, using a clever AI system, with a drawing by Munch himself By Daniel Milroy Maher 05/11/2026 3:04 am The Mu
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

New Edvard Munch exhibition utilises AI and visitor creativity

The interactive show allows visitors to create their own artworks, which are then paired, using a clever AI system, with a drawing by Munch himself

By Daniel Milroy Maher 05/11/2026 3:04 am

The Munch museum in Oslo has opened a new interactive exhibition that looks to make its vast archive of work by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch more accessible and engaging to the public. Titled Connect the Lines, this latest exhibition by the museum expands on the research and innovation of its previous project New Snow, which offered a fresh, creative way to explore Munch’s many drawings.

With an archive of over 7,000 artworks by the late artist, who was known for sketching his surroundings on an near-daily basis, the museum needed a way to showcase this significant part of his oeuvre without risking damage to the already fragile pieces. The answer came in the form of an interactive exhibition which invites visitors to engage with Munch’s work through an AI-powered creative task.

Once inside, visitors are encouraged to draw on touchscreens, composing any kind of sketch that they wish, before their finished artworks are then analysed by an AI system and matched to a corresponding sketch by Munch. The system looks for similarities in form, colour and motif and uses these parameters to create a suitable pair. As more of Munch’s sketches are connected with new ones created by visitors, the full collection of work within the archive is slowly revealed.

In order to make this activity as engaging as possible, the team at Munch also invited UK-based graphic design studio Intercity to build a visual identity for the project. In turn, Intercity came up with a striking series of designs for Connect the Lines, which enhance the overall experience.

Most notably, they created a suite of geometric background animations, mixed with organic rounded shapes, which feature across the UI. These come to life on the exhibition’s touchscreens, and change according to the type of interaction. When idle, the pattern pulses to draw attention; when visitors scroll, the pattern stretches; and when visitors share their matches, the pattern rotates.

These entrancing designs are complemented by a rich colour palette of pink, orange and green, bringing a markedly dynamic and contemporary touch to an exhibition full of static, historical works. The colours and patterns also serve as backgrounds for posters and signage around the museum, contrasting with Munch’s small character sketches, which are fondly known as ‘mascots’.

Speaking on the museum’s collaboration with Intercity, Katrine Elise Agpalza Pedersen, curator of contemporary art at Munch, said: “The design for Connect the Lines had to do far more than look good; it had to turn a digital drawing installation into a coherent experience that audiences could feel their way through.”

Along with the central drawing task, Connect the Lines also features an animation of the full digital archive of Munch’s work, as well as a live data screen at the entrance to the gallery which shows the number of visitor drawings that have been completed, and how many of Munch’s own sketches have been discovered – highlighting the unique connection that has been forged between visitor and artist.

Connect the Lines is on display at Munch Museum until November 29; munch.no

entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Boots takes a humorous approach in its Christmas ad

The spot sees various Boots products become an unexpected source of obsession to those who receive them as gifts

By Eliza Williams 04/11/2026 9:52 am

Created by WPP, the new ad is an extension of Boots’ ‘Give it Some Boots’ platform, which launched in September. It continues the playful approach of the campaign, while dialling up the humour to enjoyably ridiculous levels.

The ad begins on Christmas Day, where we see women across the nation opening gifts containing Boots products – including hair stylers, an electric toothbrush and the inevitable LED Light Therapy mask (a true gift to ad writers looking for comedy this year) – in raptures. We then see the products become full-blown obsessions in the recipients’ everyday lives.

The result is a witty ad that manages to insert tonnes of Boots products in a way that doesn’t feel boring or annoying. “Instead of following the conventions of Christmas advertising, we wanted to turn up the things that only Boots can really own – incredible beauty products, the thrill of discovery and the very human obsession that happens when you find something you absolutely love, all with our fresh energy, style and attitude,” says Simon Lloyd, deputy CCO EMEA at VML.

“This allowed us to be braver, from the comedic script down to the deliberate music choice. This isn’t simply a new Christmas campaign; it’s the next statement of intent for Boots and the kind of work we want Boots to become known for.”

entry.title: New book pays homage to the overlooked craft of bookplates
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration New book pays homage to the overlooked craft of bookplates In his latest book, Tim Sumner explores the ancient design practice, and reveals the many gems in his personal collection By Daniel Milroy Maher 04/11/2026 3:33 am British graphic designer Tim Sumner,
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

New book pays homage to the overlooked craft of bookplates

In his latest book, Tim Sumner explores the ancient design practice, and reveals the many gems in his personal collection

By Daniel Milroy Maher 04/11/2026 3:33 am

British graphic designer Tim Sumner, known for his iconic zine on paper bag ephemera, To Have and To Hold, has released a new book through his recently-founded publishing venture, Collect. Titled Bookplates No.1, it contains a carefully curated selection of the unique artworks that have historically indicated ownership of a book.

Taken from Sumner’s own collection, as well as several others, the featured bookplates span the last century, reflecting the enduring impact of this type of design. Beautiful though they may be, Sumner notes that bookplates are often “hugely overlooked pieces of graphic design”.

He continues: “I was introduced to them long ago and have collected them ever since … I find them compelling because they are bold and simple; be it a crest, a motto or a name – they are unique works of art.”

Rendered here in black and white, Sumner chose to print Bookplates No.1 using a risograph machine at his local arts studio in Hazlehurst. Not only does risograph offer a unique finish, but the budget-friendly nature of the process (compared to lithograph), allowed Sumner to invest in other aspects of the book, such as using Colorplan paper by GF Smith, and thread-sewn binding.

Explaining his creative process, Sumner says: “I wanted these elements of craft to shine through. I curated, designed, printed and bound this book, [and even] hand-cut the dust-jacket. It’s a labour of love but it’s what I enjoy about publishing. With that said, I won’t be doing this for every book. I numbered all of our paper bag archive zines by hand with a price gun, so you would think I would have learnt my lesson by now.”

Though Sumner admits that the driving force behind his curation was mostly the aesthetic appeal of each bookplate, he insists he also appreciates the sentimental aspect of creating, and using, a bookplate in the first place.

“They show that each book has importance and significance in someone’s collection,” he notes. “They are mirrors of the people who own them and the times that they lived in. Expressions of their identity, reflected on the opening page of their book – something so common, so small, yet so considered.”

Reflecting on the desired impact of this release, Sumner hopes readers simply enjoy the book, but he also loves the idea that it might inspire others to start their own collections of treasured artefacts: “Whether it’s printed media or not, collections are good and I would encourage everybody to collect something.”

Bookplates No.1 is out now via Collect Books; collect-books.com

entry.content:
Creative Process

Prince Gyasi on bringing African culture to luxury branding

The visual artist discusses his evolving creative practice, and the influence of Ghanaian culture and Afrobeats on his new partnership with Martell

By Adam Woodward 04/11/2026 3:21 am

Prince Gyasi has always had an instinct for knowing when to change direction. The self-taught Ghanaian visual artist has earned plaudits for his striking portrait photography, typically characterised by vivid blocks of colour and surreal compositions. Yet while that visual language has become increasingly recognisable, he is reluctant to let it define the limits of his practice.

“I don’t want to be put in a box, so I like to sprinkle in the different things I’m known for,” he tells CR. “My development as an artist has always been about trying to find different ways of expressing myself in response to whatever problem I’m trying to solve.”

His latest venture is with Martell, one of the world’s oldest Cognac houses, for which he has taken on the role of creative partner to develop a range of work spanning film, experiences and products, including a capsule clothing collection and limited-edition XO and VS Afrobeats bottles designed in collaboration with Nigerian-American singer-songwriter and record producer Davido.

entry.title: How do you make time for creativity when the work never stops?

entry.content:
In partnership with Dropbox
Sponsored content

How do you make time for creativity when the work never stops?

For Gravity Global, working across time zones means keeping files, feedback and ideas moving around the clock. With Dropbox, the agency is streamlining handovers and giving its creative teams more time to focus on the work

For a creative team spread across time zones, the end of the working day is someone else’s starting point. A campaign moves from one desk to another, a new cut is ready for review, or client feedback arrives while the people who need to act on it are asleep.

That rhythm can extend the working day without extending anyone’s hours. But it also makes small gaps expensive. A missing file or an unclear comment can leave the next team waiting, with nobody online to answer the question.

Gravity Global knows that challenge well. The fully remote agency brings together teams across the US, UK, Vietnam and Latin America, with work spanning campaigns, shoots and digital production. Known for its longstanding relationship with Honda Powersports, it ranked first among global B2B brand marketing agencies in the 2026 Global Agencies Benchmarking Report, with gross income of $189 million.

“We describe ourselves as a 24/6 agency,” says Jeff Robertson, who has led Gravity’s technology function since 2013. “As one team finishes its day, another is getting started. That gives us a lot of scope to keep projects moving, but only if the next team has the files and context it needs to pick up where their colleagues left off.”

Gravity’s growth through acquisitions has brought more people and capabilities into the business, making those handovers increasingly important. Teams need to use their overlapping hours to build on the work, not reconstruct what happened before they came online.

For Gravity, that starts with the handover. But the bigger ambition is to protect time for the thinking that clients actually come to an agency for.

NOBODY SHOULD START THEIR DAY LOOKING FOR YESTERDAY’S WORK

A handover can look complete until someone opens the project and discovers the latest file is still on a colleague’s computer.“If somebody forgot to upload a file at the end of their day, you’d lose an entire day’s work,” says Jeff Robertson, who has run Gravity’s technology function through several agency acquisitions since 2013.

“The next team would be ready to get started, but the files they needed would still be sitting on someone else’s computer. Across time zones, you can’t always get hold of that person straight away, so making the latest work available needs to be part of the process, rather than another task to remember before logging off.”

Automatic syncing through Dropbox helps remove that dependency. When someone saves a file in a synced folder, the update becomes available to colleagues without a separate end-of-day upload. The next team can pick up the work with fewer messages, checks and delays.

For Dave Bascand, executive creative director at Gravity, the value is in how little attention that process needs. “We want it to work in the background,” he says.

“Whether we’re saving the latest campaign files or uploading material from a shoot, colleagues elsewhere need to be able to pick it up without chasing us. When you’re working across time zones, you don’t always have the chance to explain where everything is. The handover needs to be clear enough for the next person to get started.”

That matters commercially, too. Time spent finding missing material is time a team cannot spend developing an idea or refining a piece of work.

“When the technology works perfectly, we save a huge amount of money,” Robertson says.

WHICH VERSION ARE WE ACTUALLY WORKING ON?

Getting access to a file is only part of the problem. People also need to know whether it is the right one. Like many agencies, Gravity coordinates work through Teams, Asana and email. Those conversations serve different purposes, but they can also leave people piecing together which attachment, link or update represents the latest work.

Gravity uses Dropbox as a shared source for project files, giving colleagues a consistent place to check the current version. “You can step back, go to the source and see the date on the latest version,” Bascand says. “There’s no second-guessing.”

Robertson also sees the benefit in fewer interruptions: “There aren’t endless versioning issues, people working from old files or unable to find the right one.” The same clarity needs to extend to freelancers and clients. An agency can have its internal processes in order and still lose time if an external collaborator struggles to open or share the material.

For Robertson, straightforward file sharing measurably improves the support his team provides. He says Dropbox sharing queries are rare compared with those generated by other platforms the agency has used.

“It’s usually not that other platforms don’t work,” he says. “It’s that they’re so complicated nobody can use them properly.”

Every access query adds another exchange to a project. Making sharing easier helps keep the conversation focused on the work.

FEEDBACK NEEDS SOMEWHERE TO LAND

“Can we change this bit?” is a simple request when two people are looking at the same screen. But, across teams and time zones, it can become the start of a much longer conversation.

Video feedback is particularly vulnerable. Comments arrive in separate emails, references to moments in a cut are imprecise, and an editor has to work out whether two reviewers mean the same thing. A request can be overlooked or interpreted differently from what the client intended.

Those extra exchanges cost time and money and they can also make the client experience feel harder than it needs to be.

To solve this challenge, Gravity uses Dropbox Replay to bring the feedback back to the footage. Reviewers can leave frame-accurate comments, draw on the image and mark up the timeline, making it easier to show where a change is needed.

“We use Replay particularly for our shoot material,” Bascand says. “You can leave a comment or draw a circle around exactly what you mean. Whoever picks it up, whether they’re overseas or in our production office in Minneapolis, has the feedback right there with the footage, so they can spend their time making the change instead of trying to interpret an email or waiting for someone to clarify it.”

Robertson compares it to tracking changes in a document: the feedback sits alongside the material it refers to. Previously, the team would share a link, collect comments by email, and potentially spend the next day figuring out whether everyone understood them.

“You’re eliminating entire rounds of revisions,” he says. “Without tools like Replay, each round can take three to four hours if you’re lucky, so that adds up to days.”

For clients, commenting directly on a cut makes it easier and faster to explain what they want. For the creative team, it leaves more time to respond thoughtfully, with less back-and-forth to establish what was meant.

MORE OUTPUT MAKES CREATIVE JUDGEMENT MATTER MORE

AI is adding another dimension to this challenge. While AI now lets teams produce content at speed, that output still needs to be shared, reviewed, and developed into final copy.

Gravity has already been quick to embrace AI and is positive about its potential for the creative industry. The agency uses it daily, from automating repetitive tasks to creating early visuals that help clients understand a proposed shoot.

“AI can help us bring an idea to life earlier and have a more useful conversation with the client,” says Bascand. “It gives us more possibilities to explore, especially in those early stages when we still need to decide what works, what feels right for the brand and what deserves to go further.”

But, as output grows, that human review becomes increasingly important. In a Dropbox-sponsored study of more than 500 US professionals who use AI, 40% identified accuracy and quality as a barrier to turning AI output into finished work.

“Creating more doesn’t automatically mean creating something better,” Bascand says. “You still need someone to ask: is this distinctive and does it answer the brief? Our creative judgement is what turns those possibilities into work worth putting in front of a client.”

Faster creation also brings practical challenges. Robertson recalls AI-generated dashboards remaining on colleagues’ computers, requiring the agency to find a way to share them.

“People were creating useful things quickly, but they could still end up sitting on an individual’s machine,” he says. “You need to get the right people involved so they can review it and build on it. Creating it is only the beginning.”

The same study found that 84% agreed AI helps employees create work faster than their organisation’s processes can keep up. For Gravity, clear handovers and coordinated feedback help bridge that gap, giving people a smoother path from an early idea to finished work.

GIVING IDEAS ROOM TO GET BETTER

The commercial pressure to produce more, faster, is familiar across the creative industry. But speed alone gives clients little reason to choose one agency over another.

“If everything looks the same, I don’t know what it’s worth creatively,” Bascand says. “It just becomes the same as every competitor.”

Gravity’s approach connects the practical work of syncing files, sharing versions and coordinating reviews to a bigger creative ambition. Fewer avoidable interruptions give teams more room to question an idea, explore another direction and improve what reaches the client.

“The biggest value we offer clients is our creative thinking and that’s not going to change,” Bascand says. “The point of making production more efficient is to give that thinking more room. We want people to have time to challenge an idea, try something different and make the work better, rather than use those hours chasing files or clarifying feedback.”

For a team working across four time zones, a good handover does more than keep a project moving. It gives the next person the material, clarity and space to add something worthwhile.

The file can sync automatically. The feedback can arrive in the right place. What happens next is where the agency earns its place.

entry.title: John Lewis marks 20th Christmas ad with star-studded effort
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration John Lewis marks 20th Christmas ad with star-studded effort Kristin Scott Thomas, Paul Whitehouse and Sam Fender feature in the retailer’s latest festive campaign, created by Saatchi & Saatchi, which combines traditional storytelling with a suitably theatrica
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

John Lewis marks 20th Christmas ad with star-studded effort

Kristin Scott Thomas, Paul Whitehouse and Sam Fender feature in the retailer’s latest festive campaign, created by Saatchi & Saatchi, which combines traditional storytelling with a suitably theatrical finale

By Adam Woodward 03/11/2026 7:11 am

Has the John Lewis Christmas ad, which has been a much-anticipated fixture of the season since 2007, started to lose its lustre? Perhaps in anticipation of that question, the retailer has done something it has never done before at this time of year: put a bona fide star in front of the camera.

Fresh from her latest stint as the unflappable Diana Taverner in Slow Horses, Kristin Scott Thomas faces a prospect that would test the mettle of even the head of MI5: discontented grandkids. Whereas 2025’s ad focused on a father-son relationship, and 2024 put sisters at the fore, this year’s rather more traditional effort takes John Lewis’ ‘the home of thoughtful gifting’ proposition to its logical conclusion by centring on intergenerational gifting.

According to Saatchi & Saatchi, the initial idea was rooted in the insight that grandparents often feel unsure of what to get their grandchildren, and so simply resort to stuffing a few bank notes into a card. This is illustrated by Scott Thomas’ character, Gloria, venturing into her attic in search of a vintage toy she hopes will bring her two grandkids the same joy it once brought her (spoiler: it doesn’t).

For all that this year’s ad represents a first for the brand, however, it still contains many of the tried-and-trusted elements that viewers have come to expect. Chiefly, a twinkly a cappella cover of a classic song – if anyone had a children’s choir singing You Can’t Always Get What You Want on their bingo card, congratulations.

But there is more than meets the ear: as the song continues, Sam Fender’s stirring vocal kicks in and the ad shifts up a gear. As with the re-release of Where Love Lives in 2025, Fender’s version of the Rolling Stones’ late 60s hit will be available as a limited-edition vinyl, with all proceeds going to Action for Children as part of John Lewis’ Building Happier Futures initiative. There’s a nice personal touch to the recording, too: the children performing all belong to Fender’s old school choir.

But arguably the real star of the show is neither Fender nor Scott Thomas but another national treasure: Paul Whitehouse. Voicing a pull-along wooden dog named, for the purposes of this ad, Pickles, Whitehouse brings some much-needed irreverence to proceedings, his performance dovetailing neatly with Scott Thomas’ own. Each actor is aided by a script that complements their particular talents, while lines such as “Let’s go on a montage!” (Whitehouse) provide a knowing nod to the conventions of festive advertising.

Based on a Fisher-Price toy that has been sold since 1966, Pickles is unlikely to be this year’s must-have children’s toy, but it does serve as a fitting metaphor for feeling out of touch with the younger generation. Crucially, though, the ad doesn’t end with Gloria opting to follow the latest toy fad. Instead, after embarking on a tuk tuk ride through London with Pickles, she goes back into the attic to fetch some old furnishings that turn out to be rather more interesting. Cue a dramatic turn of a key and a genuine moment of wonder when the ‘gran cave’ is revealed in all its glittering, velvet-draped glory.

Directed by Lucy Forbes for Smuggler, the film has a cinematic sensibility that helps lift it above more familiar festive ad territory. The tuk tuk scene, in particular, brings to mind the similarly chaotic night bus ride at the start of Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban – a fitting touch from Forbes, who has just wrapped on the forthcoming HBO series.

More broadly, her direction gives the film a welcome sense of scale and theatricality, ensuring that its final reveal feels like a suitably magical payoff rather than simply another exercise in Christmas sentimentality or clunky product placement. It also appears that CR’s criticism of last year’s ad was taken on board, as the on-screen talent is notably more diverse than before.

The 20th edition of the John Lewis Christmas ad may not be an instant classic, then, but it makes a convincing case for keeping certain traditions alive while allowing others to evolve with the times.

entry.title: Purple Garden rebrand centres living spiritual practices
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Purple Garden rebrand centres living spiritual practices Mother Design’s refresh transforms the psychic-services platform from a transactional experience into a calming space for long-term growth By Daniel Milroy Maher 03/11/2026 3:22 am Following Mother Desi
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Purple Garden rebrand centres living spiritual practices

Mother Design’s refresh transforms the psychic-services platform from a transactional experience into a calming space for long-term growth

By Daniel Milroy Maher 03/11/2026 3:22 am

Following Mother Design’s recent rebrand of spiritual guidance marketplace Keen, the agency has collaborated once again with its parent company Ingenio – this time on a rebrand of its other psychic services brand, Purple Garden. Whereas the Keen work aimed to entice a mainstream audience unfamiliar with spirituality, this project sees the brand appealing to ‘seasoned seekers’ instead.

Built around the creative concept of ‘A Living Practice’, the rebrand looks to reposition the platform from a destination for one-off readings to a site that facilitates long-term spiritual practice. For the team at Mother, embracing the intuition inherent in this kind of spiritual experience was key to reflecting Purple Garden’s offerings.

As such, they kicked off their creative process with a séance and chakra reading led by a Purple Garden holistic practitioner, followed by an automatic drawing and writing workshop that involved the designers working with charcoal on paper. The aim was for the team to bypass conscious thought and “step away from the screen and the rational design process”, says Mother Design creative director Joanna Tulej.

The forms, textures and feelings that emerged from this session became the raw material for the identity, drawing inspiration from artists such as Hilma af Klint and The Five, who used trance states and automatic drawing to allow imagery to surface naturally. Across Purple Garden’s assets, these organic elements are rendered using a mix of conventional design software and AI tools. The designers at Mother generated multiple iterations of the work to encourage unexpected results.

The typography follows a similar tone, revolving around a wordmark featuring elongated serifs and curved junctures that merges the modern with the whimsical. This is complemented by the typeface Literatura Present by Roman Gornitsky, with flowing descenders that add to the sense of growth, and the typeface ABC Social by Dinamo, which ensures usability on-screen.

Across the identity, the shades of purple that dominate the palette are offset by pink, maroon and grey, bringing a more dynamic feel to the aesthetic, but retaining the serene atmosphere associated with Purple Garden.

With the rebrand currently rolling out across web, advertising and social channels – soon to be followed by the app itself – Hellebuyck insists that the team at Mother “has created something that feels distinctive to Purple Garden and true to our audience, while giving us a richer and more immersive platform for the next stage of the brand”.

Finally, the Mother design team introduced “living type” to the identity, with enlarged words, inspired by cymatic patterns, which melt off the screen and reflect the way a phrase from a practitioner can stay with you and shape you long after the session has ended.

Elsewhere, imagery of objects with solarised glows and flame-like ripples depict services such as dream analysis and psychic readings, symbolising the energy passing between practitioner and customer. These are coupled with photographs that show intimate physical sensation, natural landscapes and organic textures, filtered through the brand’s purple hues to create the notion of an altered reality.

entry.content:
Creative Insight

Creating desire in the face of climate catastrophe

The climate crisis is deeply serious, but the way to engage audiences in sustainable brands doesn’t need to be – instead we should make the future feel like something worth buying into, says Ragged Edge’s Matt Smith

By Matt Smith 03/11/2026 3:02 am

The latest UN climate report makes for grim reading. The world is effectively committed to exceeding 1.5°C of global warming in the next few years. The question now is how far beyond that threshold we’ll go and whether we’ll figure out a way to pull back.

It’s a scary development. Yet with global instability and AI absorbing so much of our attention, climate change has slipped down our news feeds, even as its consequences become obvious. The climate crisis is fundamentally a systemic problem. Addressing it requires political will, regulation, infrastructure and investment on a scale that creative persuasion or individual choice can’t hope to deliver.

But consumer demand can encourage change, and branding is a tool designed to create it. For better and worse, we’re pretty good at making people want things. Yet when it comes to selling more sustainable products and services, we’ve spent a lot of time telling people what they ought to do, and not enough making them actually want to do it.

entry.title: Tesco reunites long-lost friends in heartwarming festive spot
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Tesco reunites long-lost friends in heartwarming festive spot A misplaced grocery order, a broken-down car and an unexpected reunion provide the ingredients for Tesco’s latest Christmas ad by BBH London By Rebecca Fulleylove 02/11/2026 10:12 am Created by BBH
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Tesco reunites long-lost friends in heartwarming festive spot

A misplaced grocery order, a broken-down car and an unexpected reunion provide the ingredients for Tesco’s latest Christmas ad by BBH London

By Rebecca Fulleylove 02/11/2026 10:12 am

Created by BBH London, the three-minute film, The Wrong Address, tells a tale of reconnection and forgiveness, with much of the action playing out in a Tesco delivery van.

Starring Roisin Conaty as delivery driver Polly and Anna Maxwell Martin as her old school friend Lizzie, the pair cross paths after Lizzie accidentally sends her Christmas delivery to her old address.

Now living hundreds of miles apart, the pair arrange to meet halfway to retrieve the groceries. But when Lizzie’s car breaks down, Polly steps in to help, and the two embark on an unexpected journey back to Lizzie’s new home, reminiscing and slipping back into their old friendship with ease.

The ad ends with a heartwarming embrace and the line ‘Because this Christmas, Every Little Helps’, while The Police’s Every Little Thing She Does Is Magic plays in the background.

The film was directed by Steve Rogers through Biscuit Filmworks UK x Revolver, and the initial idea was sparked by Ioulianou’s own experience of accidentally ordering hangover food to the wrong address, in that case his nan’s house.

The Wrong Address marks a return to the hero film format for Tesco, in contrast to last year’s festive campaign, which featured 11 vignettes depicting relatable Christmas scenarios in a less sugar-coated take on the season.

This year, the knowing, slightly chaotic humour of last Christmas has been swapped for a more traditional festive formula, leaning into nostalgia, friendship and the emotional pull of a feel-good reunion.

entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Richard Ayoade gets his Scrooge on for Argos Christmas ad

The comedian is spirited back to his youth courtesy of Connie the doll and Trevor the dinosaur in T&P’s latest spot for the retailer

By Adam Woodward 02/11/2026 10:12 am

British retailer Argos is building on its There’s More to Argos brand platform this holiday season with a playful twist on A Christmas Carol.

Created by T&P, Tales of Argos Past sees brand mascots Connie the doll and Trevor the dinosaur adopt the role of benevolent Christmas spirits to bring festive cheer (and a sackful of gift recommendations) to a Scrooge-like Richard Ayoade.

Directed by Declan Lowney (of Ted Lasso and Father Ted fame) through Merman, the ad transports viewers back to Ayoade’s childhood via the magic of grainy home video, where he sheds his curmudgeonly demeanour – but crucially not his natty corduroy suit and red knitted tie.

All told, it’s a fairly safe effort, and it must be said that Connie and Trevor’s shtick is starting to wear thin. It’s saved, however, by the fact that Ayoade is clearly having fun recreating moments from the novel, such as leaning out of a window to call out to a passerby; in this case an Argos delivery driver.

The product integration is nicely done, too – who else remembers circling their most sought-after items in the Argos catalogue? – and while CR is running a sweepstakes on how many of this year’s Christmas ads feature people wearing LED face masks, we’ll be surprised if any do so to better comic effect.

If nothing else, tapping into the cosy feeling of Christmas nostalgia makes perfect sense for a high street institution that has been around since 1973, but which has struggled more recently to shed its image as a glorified toy shop. Then again, Connie and Trevor’s continued presence rather does undermine the point.

When it comes to reminding consumers what this time of year is really all about, then, perhaps there is still life in the old Christmas classics. As Charles Dickens once said (probably): if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.
